seriesStmt.p: Machine readable texts of the unpublished correspondence of James Joyce

projectDesc.p: James Joyce's unpublished correspondence, collected, annotated, and made available as a digital edition

div.p: My client wishes me to write to you on the following matters:

He has inquired about the fare to Dublin and finds that this costs from London to Dublin and available for one month somewhere about £4.-.-. He therefore proposes to add to the original amount two pounds and to send it to you as soon as you decide to go and let him know about it.
Further matters are litterary literary as follows:

list.item: Chaucer. He finds the prologue to the Tales uncommonly modern and would remind you of the comment Blake made on him. In general for your purpose there might be some more use to be made of Blake especially his deification of London as compared to the deification of Dublin in the work of our friend. The opinion that Chaucer is so very typically English does not seem to, however be his (Defoe – yes).

Shakespeare. Our friend has hardly read the sonnets with attention but remembering that you know the sonnets so well he thinks you could make a good use of your knowledge by inserting some quotations or rather semiquotations of them in your text so as to make the reader aware of your knowledge, as opposed to the neglect our friend has shown to them.

Swift would agree that Ireland may have a claim on Swift just as much as she has on the Iron Duke and Lord Northcliffe but she would not stop at that and claim Blake and Fitzgerald who were born in England.

There are two aspects of Swift the man and the prose writer. In its time the opinion prevailed that nobody had written a stronger prose or more characteristic and admirable and our friend accepted this opinion for what it was worth without analysing it more closely. On reading Swift however for the purpose of his Cyclope-episode he found that this author was nothing but an ordinary language multiplied or divided by twelve as the case may have been for the purposes of his story but on the whole he uses a very simple language. Our friend however did not insist on his opinion as it would have gone against the generally admitted statement. As a man he finds him a strong stingy sentimentalist and a bore and principally a meddler and a muddler in two women’s lives.

As a personal favour he would like you when treating the subject of the Nausikaa episode to reconsider the way you have dealt with the mysteries of ladies’ toilet and to remember that some words are too sacred to be either said or written.
The Lindenhof (courtyard of the Lime trees) and Pfahlbaute (Lake dwellings) could be inserted somewhere in the description of Zürich.
In the list of paintings you could add a drawing that Augustus John has presented to my client’s wife and a portrait of his daughter by Marie Laurencin.
He is going to send you a book on dreams by André Breton.
He is still waiting for a painting of the salmon that avatar of H.C.E.

div.p: I think I have covered all the ground and please believe me

div.note: Minor typing errors have been silently corrected and handwritten additions have been silently added.
Budgen travelled to Dublin in April 1933 for research in connection with his writing of JJMU.
Budgen mentions Chaucer’s prologue in the same paragraph as Defoe (JJMU 186) and quotes Blake re London and JJ re Dublin (JJMU 318-20).
Budgen quoted JJ on Shakespeare’s sonnets in general (JJMU 180, 291); Budgen specifically quoted one sonnet (JJMU 313).

JJ reread Swift for “Cyclops”. In JJMU Budgen quoted JJ that Swift in Gulliver’s Travels “multiplies or divides by twelve” and that Swift is a “strong and stingy sentimentalist” who “meddled with and muddled up two women’s lives” (185).

Clive Hart discussed this subject in his Introduction to JJMU (xv-xvi). Paul Léon mentioned JJ's fastidious attention to female underwear in the letter to Budgen of 7 May 1933 (LIII 280), where he evasively described a book which JJ was sending to Budgen as “The Mantle of Tanit”. Ellmann's footnote to that letter notes that “Tanit (Tanith) was virgin goddess of the moon to the Carthaginians. The book, which has not been traced, was about women’s underwear”. A reference to the author of the book along with a cursory (and skeptical) description of it in an unpublished letter from Budgen to JJ of 23 June 1933 identify the book that Budgen received as Pierre Dufay's Le pantalon féminin: Un chapitre inédit de l'histoire du costume, new ed, (Paris: Charles Carrington, Librairie des Bibliophiles Parisiens, 1916), an extensive, illustrated, and footnoted history of womens' underwear.
The Lindenhof and lime trees are in JJMU 25; Pfahlbauten (stilt houses) are on JJMU 24. Léon's lack of the terminal “n” reflects the Swiss German pronunciation.
The portraits by Augustus John and Marie Laurencin are in JJMU 189.
Probably Breton's Les vases communicants (Paris: Éditions des Cahiers Libres, 1932).
